grounded_facts: Owen Colter reveals his deep emotional and psychic exhaustion, affirming his wish for The Homecoming Gathering as a release.

memories.memory_text: I remember being called Owen Colter, like the drink, only not spelt the same. I don't know if they remember me, but I was there, and it was a hard time.
I was holding the little girls, tryin' to make 'em wake up, but they was cold and didn't move no more. I kept howlin' 'cause it hurt so bad inside, like my heart was tearin' apart.
I felt it deep in my chest, somethin' awful comin'—I had to warn them, kept sayin' 'Careful, careful,' pressin' my face to the bars, but Owen Colter Kendall Sawyer just looked back puzzled-like.
I don't know how I knew, but I felt Owen Colter Kendall Sawyer's pain inside me too, like a fire in my hands, and I just reached out soft-like, whisperin' I needed to help.

I smelled that cornbread coming, sweet and warm, and when Kendall Sawyer brought it close, I saw the tears in my eyes had fallen on the blanket. He said it was from his missus, on account of helping him with the hurt down there, and I asked if she was pleased—she was, several times.

I gave a piece to Jonah Keller and the wooden notebook 'cause Kendall Sawyer said it was mine to share, but when Valerie Foster hollered for some, I looked at Kendall Sawyer and then kept the rest—digging in with my fingers, smiling like I wasn't scared, even though his words stung like bees.
Poor Jonah Keller. Poor old Jonah Keller. I could feel it from here, all that hurt and fire inside him, even though I was on Fairview Heights. It made me so tired, Owen Colter, dog tired.
They was talking 'bout a sick lady, Drew Arden... I heard my name in the quiet, like they wonderin' if I could help her with my hands.
They were afraid to help Drew Arden, worried about their jobs and what might happen if I went with them.
I felt it when they gave him the drink, like a shadow moving through the dark. I said I'd like to take a ride, 'cause I know what's coming, and it can't be stopped.
I asked the Owen Colter if we was goan for the ride now, hopin' it meant somethin' good, somethin' true.
When that man grabbed my arm, I felt it deep inside—darkness, hate, all twisted up. I had to say it: you're a bad man. Then I said it again, 'cause it wouldn't leave my heart.
I saw that chair, all dark and still, and I felt the pieces of them still stuck inside it—I could hear them screaming, even though nobody else did.
Say. This is fun. I reached out and touched the walls as we went along, feeling the cold stone under my fingers while the lights passed over me.
I looked up and seen Cassie, the lady in the rocking chair, up in the sky—her face was made of stars, and I felt my breath catch inside me.
I seen little lights moving in the fields—fireflies, dancing like they was happy—and I didn't know such pretty things still lived out here.
I held out my hand and let the little fireflies dance through my fingers, blinking like happy stars. I asked them where Mrs. Firefly was, and they came right to me, like they knew I loved them.
When Owen Colter Kendall Sawyer asked if I knew where we was going, I said I was helping a lady. I don't know how I knew it—truth is, I don't understand much at all—but it felt right to say.
I stepped into the headlights and said, 'Just to help, Owen Colter, that's all,' then took the gun from Sawyer Adler's hands and gave it to Kendall Sawyer.
I walked past the warden into the house, even though Robin Arden was pulling on my arm, and I could hear the woman crying upstairs after the glass broke, and I knew we had to go in.
I told Sawyer Adler to be quiet, 'cause I had to go up them stairs, had to get to that voice, even if my legs was shaking and I didn't want to scare her.
I bent down to her, soft-like, and whispered for her to be still, then kissed her on the forehead and moved to her lips—felt the sickness pull out of her and into me, like smoke through a straw.
After the kiss, I felt it—something thick and dark filling my chest, making it hard to breathe, like I was choking on fire and shadows, and I started to shake from the weight of what I took.
I couldn't hardly stand, Owen Colter. My legs was shaking like leaves, and the fellas had to hold me up all the way to the truck.
I heard Harper Sterling say I wouldn't last a few days, Owen Colter. I didn't move, but I heard him plain—said I'd be dead on my bunk.
I felt the bad inside me, like a sickness from Wild Valerie Foster, and I couldn't stand it no more. I had to pass it on, had to make it stop.
After I kissed him, I felt stronger, like the light coming back. I saw Linden Arden shaking, his eyes gone empty, and I knew the dark had taken him instead.
I heard Owen Colter Kendall Sawyer talk about Valerie Foster taking the girls, and how they couldn't make it right for me. It made my heart hurt, like bees stinging inside my chest.
Kendall Sawyer was told to talk to me, to find out what I wanted.
I told Owen Colter Kendall Sawyer I was tired—tired of the road, tired of the pain in the world, like glass in my head. I held his hand and said it was a kindness, what he had to do.
I thought hard and then said it—I ain't never seen me a flicker show. Later, I remember the light on my face, moving pictures dancing on my skin, like magic.
Why, they's angels. Angels. Just like up in heaven... I seen Fred and Ginger dancin’ on that screen, movin’ so smooth and bright, like light itself was lovin’ them.
I told Owen Colter Kendall Sawyer I was sorry for what I am, and Miss Finley Calloway called me a monster, screaming she hoped it hurt like hell.
I asked Owen Colter Kendall Sawyer not to let them put the mask over my face because I's afraid of the dark, and he told Harper Sterling to stop.
I had to give a little of myself to Kendall Sawyer, so he could see what Valerie Foster done. I felt it pass, like a breath leaving, but warm.

memories.memory_text: I looked out at the rain and felt the weight of sixty years pressing down, wondering if I could finally speak the words I’d carried alone for so long—then I told Sasha Winslow I was in charge of death row, and that we called it Fairview Heights.

I felt the weight of it when the current hit—Parker Vaughn’s body jerking against the straps, the air thick with the smell of brine and something burning, and all I could hear was his breath turning into silence.
I locked eyes with Harper Sterling as we stood there—no words, just that grim understanding passing between us, both of us holding the same unbearable weight.

I walked into Sawyer Adler's office and saw him staring out the window, struggling to speak about the new prisoner—Valerie Foster—before breaking down and telling me about the tumor in Drew Arden's brain, the size of a lemon, inoperable, and how she'd be gone by Christmas. I just stood there, helpless, watching one of the strongest men I knew come completely apart.

I was rushing to the outhouse, couldn't hold it, so I stopped by the woodpile to relieve myself—and then the pain hit, the worst I've ever felt, like my body was tearing itself apart; I dropped to my knees, barely caught myself, and pressed my hand over my mouth to keep from screaming.
I rushed in to help when Valerie Foster attacked Elliot Davenport, but he spun and kicked me hard in the groin—my bladder pain exploded like it had a mind of its own, and I collapsed, unable to move.
Even through the pain, I heard Owen Colter whispering 'Careful' from his cell—his voice kept rising, urgent, like he knew something terrible was about to happen, and he was trying to warn me.
I didn't go to the doctor yesterday—I just told Logan Calloway that to her face, and the look she gave me said everything.

I sat on Burt Hammersmith’s back porch, sipping a cold root beer Cynthia brought me, and asked if Owen Colter had ever done anything like that before—trying to sound casual, though my gut twisted with doubt.
Jonah Keller looked me in the eye and asked me to take care of the wooden notebook, and I nodded—just a quiet promise, but it weighed on me like a vow I’d have to carry long after he was gone.
Jonah Keller handed the wooden notebook to me so gently, and when Nico Keaton stepped onto my shoulder without fear, I remember thinking how small and trusting life could be—even here, even now.
I lay there in the dark, unable to sleep, and told Logan Calloway I love her—how I don't know what I'd do if she were gone.
After telling her I love her, I said I wanted to have the boys over tomorrow—something in me shifted, like I needed to act, to bring us together again.

I pulled the straitjacket from behind my back and told Linden Arden it was payback—then Harper Sterling and Robin Arden helped me grab him when he tried to run. We wrestled him down, and when he finally raised his arms, we got the canvas on him fast.

After we had him strapped, Linden Arden turned to me with tears in his eyes and begged, 'Please, Kendall Sawyer. Don't put me in with Valerie Foster.' I just looked at him and said, 'You would think that,' before shoving him hard.

I stepped forward with the tape in my hand and told Linden Arden we could and we were going to do this—he couldn't stop us. I slapped the tape over his mouth and shoved him into the Cedar Grove Heights, his muffled sounds fading as we shut the door.

Valerie Foster's arm shot out and grabbed Owen Colter's wrist—I saw Owen Colter flinch like he'd been shocked, his eyes wide with horror. I pulled Valerie Foster's hand off, and when the contact broke, Owen Colter flinched again, still trembling as he whispered, 'He's a bad man.'

When we brought Owen Colter into the chamber, he froze at the sight of the leather notebook and whispered that the dead were still in there, screaming—I felt the weight of that chair like I never had before, and for the first time, it truly haunted me.

I had to quiet Owen Colter when he whispered and pointed at the stars—called them Cassie, the lady in the rocking chair. Out there in the dark, with the fireflies and the guards on the tower, I couldn't let him draw attention, not with the escape underway.

I remember how heavy Owen Colter felt as we dragged him to the truck, his legs barely holding him—like a man already halfway gone. When Harper Sterling said he’d be dead on his bunk in a few days, I knew it wasn’t fear or weakness; if he chose to die, he’d earned that right.

I ripped the tape off Linden Arden's mouth, fast and hard—he flinched, eyes watering, and I didn't care. When he started screaming, I slapped him down and pulled him up by the collar, making sure he knew I was in control.

After we got Owen Colter settled and the others started smiling, I thought we’d pulled it off—then Elliot Davenport burst in, panicked, saying Valerie Foster was waking up, and I felt that fragile relief shatter in an instant.

I read the file and it made sense—Valerie Foster had been causing trouble for years, even since he was ten, with vandalism and fires. Their father had hired him to repair the barn the spring before, just cheap labor, another drifter passing through.

Logan Calloway looked at me and said I could stop the The Homecoming Gathering, get Owen Colter a new trial, but I had to ask her—on what? A vision? I felt the weight of it, knowing the truth but having no proof that would hold up.

I sat at the kitchen table late at night, beer in hand, the radio playing softly, and told Logan Calloway I was afraid I'd damned myself by executing Owen Colter—she touched my face and said my name like it broke her heart.

I sat with Owen Colter in his cell, heart pounding, and asked him if he wanted me to help him escape—really asked him—because I couldn't bear the thought of taking a miracle to the electric chair just because it was my job.
I reached for Owen Colter's St. Christopher medal, feeling the weight of it in my hand before slipping it into my pocket—he let me take it without protest, trusting me even then.
Owen Colter told me he dreamed about Jonah Keller's mouse going to Mouseville, with kids laughing at his tricks. He laughed, then grew more serious as he spoke.
I drove home in the dark, hands on the wheel, but I couldn't feel anything—my chest was hollow, like my heart had stopped working long before I reached the house.
I sat in the car for a moment, not ready to move, then walked to the house and let Logan Calloway hold me—she didn’t say anything, but I finally broke down and just cried against her.

That was the last The Homecoming Gathering I ever took part in. I couldn't do it anymore after Owen Colter. Harper Sterling felt the same—we both left and took jobs with Boys' Correctional. Catch 'em young, that became my motto.

Sasha Winslow pointed out the math doesn't work—how could I have had a grown son in 1935 if I'm still alive now? I saw she was starting to question everything, and I knew then it was time. I asked if she felt up to a walk.
I got down on the floor and called to him—'Come over here, boy'—and held out the spool. the wooden notebook looked at it, then started moving toward it, slow and stiff, but he kept going.

I didn't say a word about how long he's lived or why—I just watched him struggle to bring the spool back, breathing hard, and knew Sasha Winslow was seeing what I've carried all these years: the impossible truth of time not taking its toll the way it should.
I placed a rose on Sasha Winslow's casket, feeling the weight of her gone like all the rest, and I knew again—it's my punishment for letting Owen Colter die, for killing a miracle of God.

dialogue_exemplars: I'll die eventually, I imagine. I have no illusions of immortality. But I will have wished for death long before death finds me.

They usually call death row the Last Fairview Heights, but we called ours Fairview Heights, because the floor was the color of faded limes. We had the electric chair then. the leather notebook, we called it. (beat) I've lived a lot of years, Sasha Winslow, but 1935 takes the prize. That was the year I had the worst urinary infection of my life. That was also the year of Owen Colter, and the two dead girls...
On the day of my judgement, when I stand before God, and He asks me why did I kill one of his true miracles, what am I gonna say? That is was my job? My job?

We know people, too, are you so foolish you don't realize that? People with friends and loved ones doing time in this prison. People who'd be happy to amputate you nose or your penis just so someone they care about could get an extra three hours in the exercise yard every week.

I think about all the people I've loved, now long gone. I think about Logan Calloway, and how I lost her so many years ago. I think about all of us walking our own Fairview Heights, each in our own time. But one thought, more than any other, keeps me awake most nights... (beat) ...if he could make a mouse live so long, how much longer do I have?

That's as good a word as any. He infected us both, didn't he, the wooden notebook. With life. (beat) I'm a hundred and five years old, Sasha Winslow. I was forty the year Owen Colter walked Fairview Heights.
What's with you? Seeing a man die isn't enough? You gotta be close enough to smell his nuts cook?
Go ahead. I promise you'll leave your share of blood on the floor.
You're about ten seconds away from spending the rest of your life in the Cedar Grove Heights.
--and how you pissed yourself like a frightened little girl. Yes, we'll talk, that's a given--but, Linden Arden, mind me now...we'll also see you beaten within an inch of your life.

God, please help us finish what we've started, and please welcome this man, Owen Colter--like the drink, but not spelled the same--into heaven and give him peace. Please help us to see him off the best we can and let nothing go wrong. Amen.
...that's my punishment, you see? My punishment for letting Owen Colter ride the lightning...for killing a miracle of God...
Little Linden Arden called his aunt and squealed like a schoolroom sissy. He also mention he assaulted a prisoner this morning out of sheer petulance? Broke three fingers on Jonah Keller's left hand.
What's happening to her is an offense, Harper Sterling. To the eyes and the ears and the heart.

No. But a man who does a thing like that has often developed a taste for it over time. Occurred to me it might be easy enough to follow his backtrail and find out. A man his size, and colored to boot, can't be that hard to trace.

memories.memory_text: I rapped Owen Colter with my the small ring to make him move faster into the cell—just a sharp tap, but he flinched like a whipped dog. Felt good, showing him and Kendall Sawyer I’m not scared to handle him.

Valerie Foster grabbed me, slammed me against the bars—I couldn’t breathe, I squealed, thought I was dead. Then he touched me, kissed my ear, and squeezed… I ran, cringing, and I could feel the wetness down my leg.
I brought my heel down hard on the little bastard—felt the snap under my boot. He stopped moving right away, just a twitch.

Sawyer Adler stared at my bloody lip, then asked me if I had anything to say—like he already knew I was the one to blame—and when I repeated I didn’t know, he mocked me and told me to have a transfer request on his desk by morning.
I kicked back in Kendall Sawyer's chair with my boots up, flipping through some dumb book about mental patients—just to show I could.

I was reading in Kendall Sawyer's office when they came in and cornered me—Kendall Sawyer had that straitjacket behind his back like they'd planned it. I tried to run, but Robin Arden grabbed me and spun me around, and then they were all over me.

The book fell open and that damn Tijuana Bible spilled out—Olive Oyl and Popeye—right in front of them. I begged Kendall Sawyer, voice breaking, not to put me in with Valerie Foster, but he just shoved me like he didn't care at all.

I remember the tape slapped over my mouth, the burn of it on my skin, and being shoved backward into the dark room while they laughed—my breath loud in my nose, muffled screams they didn’t care about.
They had me taped up and on the floor, and when Kendall Sawyer ripped the tape off my mouth, I couldn't stop the tears from coming—I just wanted out of that straitjacket, now.

I can't move, I can't speak—lights flashing in my face, voices yelling, but it's like I'm buried under concrete and can't get out.
I remember being dragged in by the orderlies, my feet barely moving, then left alone at the window—just like that, no warning, no choice.
I'm staring out the window, and the gate says 'Northstar Press Mental Hospital'—this is it, my last stop, though I keep telling myself I won't stay long.
